REASONS FOR ORDER
LEBLANC J.A.

[1] The Court once again has before it a motion from the appellant, who is currently in custody at the Cowansville penitentiary in Quebec (the Institution), seeking to obtain orders regarding the tools that he believes Correctional Service Canada (CSC) should make available to him so that he may adequately prepare this appeal.

[2] The first motion to this effect and subsequent requests for reconsideration were denied by this Court on July 7 and August 25, 2022 (the Orders), given that the Court was satisfied, upon consideration of all the evidence in the record at the time and the state of the law on the subject, that the appellant had not shown that he was deprived of [translation] “reasonable access to legal sources and texts, to a computer, to printing services and to means of communication that would allow him to represent himself before the Court” and that the increased access he was seeking “could compromise the legitimate security requirements that characterize the prison environment and the reasonable limitations that this environment imposes (Barkley v. Canada, 2017 FCA 7 at paras. 2–3 and 9; Pengelly v. Canada (Attorney General), 2005 FC 693 at paras. 11–12)”.

[3] The appellant is back with this motion based on the fact that the laptop computer that he had been authorized to use starting in autumn of 2021 was seized by members of the Institution on November 29, 2022. He is therefore requesting that this Court restore his access to this laptop.

[4] However, he is also seeking that which was denied him under the Orders, namely, access to a hard drive and legal search engines to carry out the case law research required for this appeal. In the absence of any new facts—and, relative to the evidence that was before this Court at the time the Orders were issued, I have not detected any new facts—these submissions cannot succeed because, in this respect, this motion is a roundabout way of appealing the Orders. This is simply not allowed.

Justice Pamel also made an error in law by not consulting or referring to other case law applicable to file T-2189-14 that reflects an entirely different reality regarding the amounts awarded in damages, as well as exemplary and punitive damages awarded in judgments concerning cases and situations that are similar to this case.

[6] The appellant did not follow either of these instructions. As we will see, this will influence the outcome of this motion.

[7] Therefore, the only new fact that could justify a new motion is the seizure in late November 2022 of the laptop computer loaned to the appellant by CSC. The appellant also submits that during a telephone conversation in December 2022, one of the respondent’s solicitors allegedly admitted in some manner that CSC had deliberately interfered with the procedures it had put in place for him to obtain the support required to prepare this appeal. From this, the appellant concludes that the respondent is guilty of perjury and deliberately obstructing the administration of justice.

[8] A preliminary remark is needed in connection with this new proceeding: it extends far beyond the scope of this appeal, given that the appellant’s complaint focuses on his limited means for carrying out not only this appeal, but a whole series of judicial and administrative proceedings before the Federal Court, the Canadian Human Rights Commission, the Office of the Correctional Investigator and the Access to Information and Privacy Office. There is nothing specific in terms of his ability to conduct this appeal, particularly in light of the subject of his appeal—the quantum of damages awarded to him by the Federal Court—and the instructions, referred to above, that the appellant ignored.

[9] But before getting to the heart of the matter, I must first settle several procedural issues. The appellant has prepared a reply record in response to the record filed by the respondent in reply to his new motion. However, as was the case with the proceedings that gave rise to the Orders, this reply relies on evidence which, to be presented, required leave from the Court to be given in advance upon proof of “unusual circumstances”. This was not done, contrary to the principle that an applicant cannot split its case by presenting a reply with the aim of enhancing its main evidence (Amgen Canada Inc. v. Apotex Inc., 2016 FCA 121 at paras. 7 and 11–12).

[10] Given these irregularities, the appellant’s reply record was not formally filed in this record by the Registry, which sought the direction of this Court. Meanwhile, the respondent filed a Notice of Motion seeking leave to present two supplementary affidavits and a reply to the appellant’s reply record. Alternatively, the respondent seeks the striking out of the [translation] “new allegations and new exhibits that the appellant included in his reply to the respondent’s reply without having obtained advance leave from the Court”.

[11] The appellant then filed a reply record—containing new affidavits and new exhibits—to the motion brought by the respondent.

[12] It would have been preferable for the respondent to object to the filing of the reply record, as it had done during the previous proceedings that gave rise to the Orders, and to await the Court’s directions regarding the outcome regarding the said record. Unfortunately, the respondent’s choice has led to both parties filing supplementary motion records, which have themselves led to letters being sent to the Registry.

[13] Regardless, it seems to me that in the particular circumstances of this case, to prevent further delays in this proceeding, the solution that adheres best to the letter and the spirit of the Federal Courts Rules in general and with regard to motions submitted to this Court in particular—which must be determined strictly on the basis of written submissions—is to circumscribe the appellant’s reply record to remove the evidence and the new allegations, and therefore, to grant the alternative relief of the respondent’s motion.

[14] The appellant is therefore permitted to file the reply record, but for the purposes of this motion, paragraphs 10, 11, 13, 14, 17, 19 to 21, 47 to 50, 52 to 61 and 111 to 116 of the document will not be taken into account, nor will the exhibits—of which there are four—attached to it. It follows that the main relief sought by the respondent in its motion—that two supplementary affidavits be filed along with written submissions in connection with the filing of these affidavits—is now moot and, as a result, will not be given effect. The same is true for the appellant’s reply record to this motion, which is now moot because it is directly linked to the possible filing by the respondent of these two supplementary affidavits and the written submissions stemming from this filing.

[15] I will therefore return to the actual merits of the motion before the Court, which rests on the—new—fact that, on November 29, 2022, the laptop that CSC had made available to the appellant starting in the fall of 2021 was seized. According to the evidence in the record, this laptop, which was loaned to the appellant during the pandemic because access to the Institution library was limited at that time, was seized during a monthly search of the inmates’ cells. In this case, the search was moved forward after the appellant was observed in his cell watching a pornographic video on the laptop, an activity that is not authorized by the Commissioner’s Directives. During this search, the guards allegedly also found [translation] “a number of contraband peripheral computing devices” (USB keys, Micro SD cards and a hard drive), which are prohibited items within the meaning of the Corrections and Conditional Release Act.

[16] A serious disciplinary offence report was written in connection with this seizure, but it was dismissed as it was past the time limit. However, the laptop remained seized. According to the evidence in the record, solutions were allegedly proposed to the appellant between December 12, 2022, and February 8, 2023, to make it possible for him to recover the documents he had saved on the laptop in connection with all of the litigations to which he is a party. At the time, the appellant was given the choice to:
(a)sort the contents of the laptop himself, in front of a member of the Institution’s personnel, and transfer the evidence onto one peripheral device and the pleadings and his other work documents onto another device;
(b)have the solicitor representing him at that time perform this task;
(c)carry out this task himself and transfer the above-mentioned documents onto a single peripheral device, which he would be able to access himself (or through his solicitor), subject to certain conditions, and which he could keep in a secured locker, to which only he would have access, in the Institution library.

[17] In a letter to one of the respondent’s solicitors dated February 10, 2023, the appellant objected to the solutions put forward by CSC. His objections do not so much stem from the fact that the solutions are unsatisfactory, but rather from the fact that CSC still refuses to give him access to an external hard drive—or USB key—in his cell and at all times, even though such access, which does not threaten the confidentiality of the information stored on the hard drive, has been provided by CSC to a certain number of inmates at the Institution. The appellant also reiterated his accusations of perjury and obstruction of justice against CSC.

[18] According to the evidence in the record, only 3 of the 400 inmates in the Institution have laptop computers on loan from CSC in their cells, and there are only 2 in all of the other CSC penitentiaries in the Quebec Region. What these 3 inmates of the Institution have in common is the fact that they are still involved in ongoing criminal proceedings, which guarantees them the constitutionally protected right to make full answer and defence.

[19] The evidence also shows that actions were taken to ensure a privacy filter was in place when inmates consulted their documents on the computers made available to inmates in the Institution library. Furthermore, a project is reportedly underway in the various CSC institutions to allow digital peripheral devices to be used from these computers. The evidence also shows that having computers in CSC institutions creates serious security-related and operational challenges, requiring that, as a general rule, inmates be given access only in secure, controlled areas, such as in the institutional libraries. Lending laptops to inmates and allowing them to keep them in their cells is still the exception, not the rule.

[20] In light of these security requirements and the results of the search of the appellant’s cell on November 29, 2022, the CSC’s reticence about giving him access to a laptop again seems reasonable in my view, as do the alternative solutions proposed to the appellant to allow him access to the information saved on his laptop in a more controlled setting. Admittedly, the appellant does not consider these solutions optimal, but they are justified given the legitimate security requirements that characterize the prison environment and the reasonable limitations that this environment imposes.

[21] Regardless, as we have seen, the appellant wanted to strike a kind of bargain using his acceptance of the alternative solutions proposed by the respondent to demand that he be provided with a hard drive, even though that has already been refused and this Court has endorsed the refusal in the Orders. As I mentioned previously, this motion cannot, in the absence of new facts, serve as a disguised appeal of the Orders.

[22] Do the allegations of perjury and obstruction of justice alter the situation? The answer is no. The respondent’s solicitor, to whom the appellant attributes the compromising admissions, signed an affidavit relating a completely different story than that provided by the appellant. This type of allegation is very serious, as it can attract the criminal liability of the person who has been accused. Contradictory evidence is not enough to establish the merits of such allegations, nor is it insufficient to rely on how the appellant may have interpreted his conversation with the respondent’s solicitor and the legal conclusions he may have drawn from it.

In his judgement, Justice Pamel made erred in law by not carrying out a full and proper reading and interpretation of the varied case law he referred to, thereby erring in law. Justice Pamel also made an error in law by not consulting or referring to other case law applicable to file T-2189-14 that reflects an entirely different reality regarding the amounts awarded in damages, as well as exemplary and punitive damages awarded in judgments concerning cases and situations that are similar to this case.

[24] As I said previously, the present motion record contains nothing to this effect and paints a bigger picture of the appellant’s situation that goes well beyond the proceedings related to this appeal, whereas this is the sole issue this Court is empowered to dispose of in this case. In other words, this Court is missing relevant information that would have made it possible to fully grasp the appellant’s real needs in terms of preparing this appeal and the real impact that the seizure of his laptop has had on these needs. It was the appellant’s duty to provide this information, at the direction of this Court. In and of itself, the absence of this information would be grounds enough to dismiss the motion, in my view.

[25] This Court is not required to decide whether the volume of files that the appellant causes to be brought before the courts or administrative decision-makers justifies particular needs in terms of access to tools for preparation. This question may always be debated through the grievance procedure set out in the Corrections and Conditional Release Act. But within the limited scope of this file, this Court is not the appropriate forum for doing so.

[26] For all of these reasons, this motion will be dismissed, and as the respondent is not seeking costs, none shall be awarded. The filing of the appellant’s reply will be allowed, but only in the circumscribed form described in paragraph 14 of these reasons. With regard to the respondent’s motion, the alternative component of the motion is allowed, but not the main component as it is now moot. The filing of the appellant’s reply record to this motion will be allowed, but it is now moot because it is directly linked to the main component of said motion.

Meanwhile, the respondent filed a Notice of Motion seeking leave to present two supplementary affidavits and a reply to the appellant’s reply record. Alternatively, the respondent seeks the striking out of the [translation] “new allegations and new exhibits that the appellant included in his reply to the respondent’s reply without having obtained advance leave from the Court”.

Unfortunately, the respondent’s choice has led to both parties filing supplementary motion records, which have themselves led to letters being sent to the Registry.

[13] Regardless, it seems to me that in the particular circumstances of this case, to prevent further delays in this proceeding, the solution that adheres best to the letter and the spirit of the Federal Courts Rules in general and with regard to motions submitted to this Court in particular—which must be determined strictly on the basis of written submissions—is to circumscribe the appellant’s reply record to remove the evidence and the new allegations, and therefore, to grant the alternative relief of the respondent’s motion.

According to the evidence in the record, this laptop, which was loaned to the appellant during the pandemic because access to the Institution library was limited at that time, was seized during a monthly search of the inmates’ cells. (a)sort the contents of the laptop himself, in front of a member of the Institution’s personnel, and transfer the evidence onto one peripheral device and the pleadings and his other work documents onto another device;
(b)have the solicitor representing him at that time perform this task;
(c)carry out this task himself and transfer the above-mentioned documents onto a single peripheral device, which he would be able to access himself (or through his solicitor), subject to certain conditions, and which he could keep in a secured locker, to which only he would have access, in the Institution library.

[17] In a letter to one of the respondent’s solicitors dated February 10, 2023, the appellant objected to the solutions put forward by CSC. [18] According to the evidence in the record, only 3 of the 400 inmates in the Institution have laptop computers on loan from CSC in their cells, and there are only 2 in all of the other CSC penitentiaries in the Quebec Region. The evidence also shows that having computers in CSC institutions creates serious security-related and operational challenges, requiring that, as a general rule, inmates be given access only in secure, controlled areas, such as in the institutional libraries. Lending laptops to inmates and allowing them to keep them in their cells is still the exception, not the rule.

[20] In light of these security requirements and the results of the search of the appellant’s cell on November 29, 2022, the CSC’s reticence about giving him access to a laptop again seems reasonable in my view, as do the alternative solutions proposed to the appellant to allow him access to the information saved on his laptop in a more controlled setting. [21] Regardless, as we have seen, the appellant wanted to strike a kind of bargain using his acceptance of the alternative solutions proposed by the respondent to demand that he be provided with a hard drive, even though that has already been refused and this Court has endorsed the refusal in the Orders. In other words, this Court is missing relevant information that would have made it possible to fully grasp the appellant’s real needs in terms of preparing this appeal and the real impact that the seizure of his laptop has had on these needs. [26] For all of these reasons, this motion will be dismissed, and as the respondent is not seeking costs, none shall be awarded. The filing of the appellant’s reply will be allowed, but only in the circumscribed form described in paragraph 14 of these reasons. With regard to the respondent’s motion, the alternative component of the motion is allowed, but not the main component as it is now moot. The filing of the appellant’s reply record to this motion will be allowed, but it is now moot because it is directly linked to the main component of said motion.
“René LeBlanc”
J.A.
